# How to write a Middle Management theme

<!-- Generated by dev/theme-guide.ts from dev/theme-guide.template.md. Edit those, not this file. -->

This guide is for you, the assistant writing the theme. Read it once from top to bottom before you write anything. The tables come straight from the extension's code, so the keys, limits and defaults here are exact.

## 1. What a theme is

Middle Management is a VS Code extension that shows AI coding sessions as pixel-art workers in a small office. The user is the manager. A theme restyles that office for a setting of the user's choice: a spaceship crew, a bakery, a lighthouse.

- A theme is one JSON object in a file named `<name>.theme.json`. The user's own themes live in their themes folder, `~/.middle-management/themes` unless the user says otherwise.
- The Front desk lists every theme in that folder under **Theme > Your offices**, using the theme's `name` and `description`. The user picks it there.
- While the office is visible it re-reads the active theme file every 2 seconds, so a saved change shows up within a couple of seconds.
- Every field is optional. Leave something out and the built-in value stays.
- A field with a problem is skipped and reported, and the rest of the file still applies. If the file is not valid JSON, the office keeps the last good theme.

**What a theme can change:** the wall sign, everyone's names and job titles, every line anyone says, how every person looks, and the colours of the rooms, furniture, windows and lights.

**What it cannot change:** the floor plan, the furniture and its shapes, the props on each desk, and the text of panels, menus and buttons. A few functional messages, such as the update notice, also stay fixed. Don't promise the user any of these.

## 2. Top-level fields

{{FIELDS_TABLE}}

Use only these keys. Unknown keys are dropped (and inside `lines`, `titles` and `colors` they are reported as errors). Don't add a `$schema` line: files named `*.theme.json` are checked against the schema automatically.

## 3. lineMode: add or replace

`lineMode` decides what your lines do to the built-in ones.

- `"add"` (the default) mixes your lines in with the built-in lines. Use it for a light touch on the ordinary office.
- `"replace"` uses only your lines, but only in the pools you fill. A pool you leave out keeps its built-in lines, so nobody ever goes silent.

**Use `"replace"` for any themed office, and fill every pool.** A pool you skip falls back to ordinary office lines, and a ship's engineer talking about the photocopier breaks the spell.

- `smallTalk` follows `lineMode` too: in replace mode your pairs are the whole water cooler.
- A staff member's own `lines` are always that person's own chat openers. `lineMode` does not affect them.
- Every pool is shuffled like a deck: no line repeats until all of its lines have been said. In replace mode a small pool therefore repeats sooner. That is why the suggested counts below matter.

## 4. Line pools

Put pools under `"lines"`, keyed by the pool name. A **lines** pool is a list of strings. A **pairs** pool is a list of `[opener, reply]` arrays: the first person says the opener and someone else answers with the reply.

```json
"lines": {
  "bossVisit": ["Charts look good. Which way is up?", "Keep that lamp burning!"],
  "itFixerTalk": [["Foggy out. Good day for cables.", "Every day is a good day for cables."]]
}
```

Each pool holds at most {{LIMIT_LINES}} entries, and each line at most {{LIMIT_LINE}} characters. "Built-in" is how many lines the office ships with. "Suggested" is how many to write in replace mode so the pool does not repeat too often.

{{POOLS_TABLE}}

Notes on particular pools:

- `bossSnoop`, `receptionAttending` and `itFix` are said once per event, so one to three lines is plenty. Each must still make sense on its own every time.
- `chatReplies` answer a staff member's own opener (their `lines`), which can be about anything. Write general reactions that fit any remark: "Ha. Fair.", not a reply to one particular joke.
- `itTalkReplies` answer either IT opener. Keep them puzzled and general.
- `itComebacks` are said by the AI worker whose screen was just fixed, not by the IT crew.
- `bossSulkStart`, `bossSulk` and `bossSulkEnd` follow one story: another agent borrows the manager's office for a while, the manager waits outside, then gets it back.

## 5. smallTalk: the water cooler

`smallTalk` is a top-level list of `[opener, reply]` pairs. Two idle workers meet, one says the opener and the other answers with the reply. This is the chatter people see most often, so give it the most lines.

- The built-in set has {{SMALL_TALK_COUNT}} pairs. You can give at most {{LIMIT_SMALL_TALK}}; aim for {{SMALL_TALK_SUGGESTED}}.
- Any two workers may say a pair, so don't name a particular speaker in it.
- Make the reply land: a twist, a dry answer or an escalation. Avoid a reply that only agrees.

```json
"smallTalk": [
  ["Did the fog horn go off again?", "Twice. Once for a ship, once for a cow."],
  ["Who keeps moving the logbook?", "The logbook moves itself. It wants to be read."]
]
```

## 6. titles

Job titles appear on tooltips and in the roster. Each is at most {{LIMIT_TITLE}} characters. Set all of them for a themed office.

{{TITLES_TABLE}}

## 7. People

### The manager and the receptionist

- `manager` is the user's own character, the boss. `{ "name", "look" }`. A name here overrides the user's own manager-name setting, so leave `name` out if the user wants to keep theirs.
- `receptionist` sits at the front desk in the lobby all day. Clicking her opens the Front desk. `{ "name", "look" }`.
- Both also accept a legacy `lines` list (see section 11). Use the pools instead.

### Side characters

`cleaner`, `vendor` (pushes the food trolley), `itFixer` and `itCritic` (the IT pair who reboot a stuck worker's screen) each take `{ "name", "look" }`. Their lines are pools in `lines`. Each starts from its built-in look: the cleaner's tabard, headband and yellow gloves, the vendor's paper hat and apron, the IT pair's outfits. Colour fields (`hair`, `shirt`, `outer`, `sleeve`, `accent`, `pants`, `shoes`, `glasses` and so on) change only that colour, and the costume stays. Setting `head` swaps the head and hair style, so the cleaner's headband goes with it. Setting `outfit` swaps the torso style, so the tabard or apron goes too. `build`, `skirt`, `shortSleeves` and `belt` swap their parts in the same way. Some things always stay, whatever the theme sets: the cleaner's bucket, the IT fixer's slouch and the IT critic's high waist. To keep a character recognisable, change colours first and only swap `head` or `outfit` when the setting needs it.

### staff

Up to {{LIMIT_STAFF}} desk workers. Entry `i` is desk slot `i`; sessions take desks in slot order as they start. Each entry takes:

- `name` (at most {{LIMIT_NAME}} characters). A worker without a name shows no name.
- `role`, their job title (at most {{LIMIT_ROLE}} characters).
- `look` (section 8).
- `lines`: that person's own chat openers, at most {{LIMIT_LINES}}. A worker uses one at most once every 40 minutes to start a water-cooler chat, and the other worker answers with a `chatReplies` line. Write a few per person, in that person's voice.

Use `{}` to leave a slot as it is: `"staff": [{}, {}, { "name": "Ida Penhallow" }]` changes only slot 3. Fill all {{LIMIT_STAFF}} slots for a themed office.

{{SLOTS_TABLE}}

Each slot keeps its built-in desk props whatever look you give it.

**Leave `pin` out.** A staff entry can carry a `pin` that ties a project to a desk. It is personal to the user's own projects, so never invent one, and keep any pin that is already in a file you are editing.

### temps

Up to {{LIMIT_TEMPS}} looks for temps, the short-lived helper agents. `{ "name", "look" }` only; temps have no lines or roles of their own. They are handed out in turn, so the seventh temp reuses the first look. `{}` keeps a slot as it is.

## 8. Looks

A `look` is an object of optional keys. Anything you leave out comes from that person's built-in look. Colours are `#rrggbb`.

**Builds** (`build`): {{BUILDS}}.

**Skin tones** (`skin`): {{SKINS}}.

**Colours**

{{LOOK_COLOURS_TABLE}}

**Switches** (`true` or `false`)

{{LOOK_SWITCHES_TABLE}}

Tips:

- Give every person a distinct silhouette: a different head style and outfit, then colours. Two people with the same head and outfit look like twins from across the room, whatever their colours.
- Mix builds and skin tones across the cast.
- Dress people for the setting: a lighthouse keeper in a dark `vest` with `"belt": true`, a cook in a white `plain` top.
- Keep hair, shirt and outer clothing apart in lightness, or the figure reads as one blob at pixel size.

## 9. Colours

`colors` recolours the office. Each key takes one `#rrggbb` colour; lighter and darker shades are worked out from it, so one colour per key is enough. Leave a key out and the built-in colour stays. "Front desk label" is what the user sees on the Front desk's Colours tab.

{{COLOURS_TABLE}}

Tips:

- The sign must be readable: keep `signText` and `signBranch` far apart in lightness from `signPlate`. Light lettering on a dark plate is safest.
- Make the floors distinct from the walls, and the desks distinct from the carpet under them, or furniture vanishes into the floor.
- Pick a coherent palette of 3 to 5 hues for the whole office, plus near-neutrals. Recolour every key that would otherwise look like a beige office in your setting, usually most of them.
- Keep `sky` and `skyline` believable through a window: the skyline sits in front of the sky, so it needs to be darker or more muted.
- `outside` is the dark strip around the building. Keep it dark.

## 10. Writing rules

These apply to every line, name, title and the sign.

- **Printable ASCII only**, characters 32 to 126. The pixel font draws anything else as `?`. That means straight quotes (`'` and `"`), a plain hyphen, three full stops for an ellipsis, and no emoji, curly quotes, en or em dashes, ellipsis characters or accented letters.
- **About 70 characters or fewer** per line; {{LIMIT_LINE}} is the hard limit. A speech bubble shows 3 rows of about 24 characters and cuts off the rest. Most good lines fit in 2 rows, about 40 characters.
- **No line breaks** inside a line.
- **Be specific to the setting.** Every line should mention or imply something from that world: its tools, its weather, its jobs, its food, its jargon. A line that would fit any office is a wasted line.
- **Vary the lengths**: some two-word lines, some full sentences.
- **Gentle humour.** Dry, warm and silly beats cruel or crude. No swearing, nothing mean about real groups of people.
- **In character, in the moment.** The "When" column of the pools table says what is happening as each line is said. A `deskBumped` line is someone losing their desk; a `cartCalls` line is a trolley vendor shouting about food. Give each speaker a consistent voice.
- **Don't repeat yourself.** No two lines the same, and no line that is just another with one word swapped.
- **Original material only.** No characters, names or catchphrases from TV, film, books or games. No real people. No real companies, brands or products. Invent every name.

## 11. Legacy fields

`manager.lines` and `receptionist.lines` still work. The manager's lines go into `bossVisit`, and the receptionist's into all three of `receptionPhone`, `receptionGreeting` and `receptionIdle`. For a new theme, use `lines.bossVisit` and the reception pools instead: they put each line in the right moment. When editing an old theme that uses them, leave them alone unless the user asks.

## 13. Checklist before you save

- [ ] The file is valid JSON: double quotes, no trailing commas, no comments.
- [ ] Only keys from this guide. Pool, title and colour keys are spelled exactly as in the tables.
- [ ] `name` (at most {{LIMIT_NAME}} characters) and `description` (one sentence, at most {{LIMIT_DESCRIPTION}}) are set.
- [ ] `"lineMode": "replace"` for a themed office, and every pool in section 4 is filled at its suggested count.
- [ ] `smallTalk` has {{SMALL_TALK_SUGGESTED}} pairs, each an array of exactly two strings.
- [ ] Every title is set, and so are the names and looks of the manager, receptionist, side characters, staff and temps.
- [ ] At most {{LIMIT_STAFF}} staff and {{LIMIT_TEMPS}} temps. No `pin` you invented.
- [ ] Every colour is `#rrggbb`. The sign lettering stands out from its plate, and the floors from the walls.
- [ ] Every string is printable ASCII, has no line breaks and is at most {{LIMIT_LINE}} characters (aim for 70). Names are at most {{LIMIT_NAME}} characters, titles {{LIMIT_TITLE}} and roles {{LIMIT_ROLE}}.
- [ ] No two lines are the same, and none borrows a name or catchphrase from existing fiction, a real person or a brand.
- [ ] Read the saved file back to confirm it is what you meant to write.
